pages.author: Józef Tomasz Rostafiński
pages.text:
The results obtained by him in this work are of three kinds: first, they concern the systematics of slime molds; further, the history of their development; and finally, their placement in the chain of organic beings.

Regarding the first point, through microscopic investigations, he discovered new characteristics for the genera established by Elias Magnus Fries, while simultaneously laying the foundations for a new system. Furthermore, he proved that certain slime molds from Fries's Aethalini group are not single sporangia but aethalia, formed from the fusion and complication of numerous individual sporangia.

pages.author: Józef Tomasz Rostafiński
pages.text:
This wrinkling is, however, entirely superficial. Not only in this instance, but generally in aethalia, it happens that during maturation, masses of protoplasm crawl over the surface of the aethalium in the form of irregularly branching veins connected into a network. During complete maturation, these stiffen in this state and subsequently dry out, covering the true cortex. This also occurs in the present case, namely in the giant rulik. Its true surface is speckled with tiny but extremely dense papillae, covered only by the stiffened masses of that net-like protoplasm. The spores in mass vary in color: they are dirty yellow in the giant rulik, olive-clay in the conical rulik, and highly variable in the clustered rulik. In the latter case, they may be pink, violet-red, dirty yellow, straw-yellow, or almost colorless. A hypothallus is found only in the giant rulik, but it is very strongly developed. It can be several millimeters thick, and in hanging forms, it transitions into a more or less cylindrical elongation up to 3 centimeters long and 1/2 centimeter wide.

Its structure is very interesting but very difficult to describe. At the very bottom usually lies a layer of hardened, black-brown, amorphous protoplasm. From this layer upward go numerous layers of many slightly wavy skins that touch each other in many places, forming numerous horizontally elongated vesicles, not closed on all sides. These are either empty or filled with granular, nut-colored protoplasm. This structure repeats further upward, with the difference that the membranes lying upon one another join into vesicles that are no longer horizontally elongated but more or less rounded. These are also not closed on all sides, often having ragged walls that extend into fibers or sheets of membrane. In short, a tissue arises here that is completely similar to that found in the male organs microsporangia of certain ferns specifically the microsporangium in Salvinia and Azolla. We shall now proceed to familiarize ourselves with the structure of the cortex. As early as the last century, Haller discovered that it has a double wall. Subsequently, Corda Corda, loc. cit., vol. V, p. 61 examined it with a microscope, but in a dry state. Therefore, he was deceived by the superficial appearance it presents in such a state and described it as consisting of an amorphous mass permeated throughout by numerous thin, net-like branching channels.

pages.author: Józef Tomasz Rostafiński
pages.text:
De Bary was the first to discover reference 7 that within their protoplasm pierwoszcznia there are tiny, highly light-refractive, and colored granules which, as he supposes reference 8, become embedded in the walls of the mature sporangia zarodnia.

Aside from the old but still vigorous monograph by Schrader, we possess no closer details regarding this group of slime molds, although their structure is among the most peculiar and otherwise unencountered forms.
